Lesson 0009 · Silmulator · from issue #18, commit 58b7e2d

ADC Transfer Functions: the Reference as the Unit of Measure

Why this matters: an ADC code is not a voltage — it is a ratio against the selected reference. Until commit 58b7e2d the MSP430 model hardcoded 3.3 V, so every reference-scaling bug in user code was invisible to SIL tests.

Sections:
☐ 1. A code is a ratio
☐ 2. The transfer function
☐ 3. The fix (58b7e2d)
☐ 4. The fixed reference set
☐ 5. Full scale & LSB
☐ 6. Why SIL cares
☐ 7. Misconceptions
☐ 8. Quiz
☐ 9. Scenarios

1. An ADC Code Is a Ratio, Not a Voltage

The single most important idea in this lesson: the number an ADC returns has no voltage unit attached to it. A 12-bit ADC answers exactly one question — "what fraction of the reference span is the input sitting at?" — quantised into 4096 steps.

The reference voltage is the unit of measure. Reading code 2047 tells you the input is at roughly half the reference — and nothing more. Half of what depends entirely on which reference was selected when the conversion ran:

Code returnedSelected reference (VR+)Actual input voltage
20471.2 V (internal VREF)≈ 0.60 V
20472.5 V (internal VREF2.5)≈ 1.25 V
20473.3 V (AVCC)≈ 1.65 V

Same code, three different physical voltages. Conversely, the same input voltage produces different codes under different references:

InputReference (VR+)Code (12-bit)Meaning
1.2 V1.2 V (VREF)4095Full scale — input equals the reference
1.2 V2.0 V (VREF2.0)245760% of span
1.2 V2.5 V (VREF2.5)196548% of span
1.2 V3.3 V (AVCC)1489≈36% of span
💡 The mental model
Think of the reference as a ruler. The ADC reports "the input reaches the 1489th tick mark of my 4096-tick ruler." If you swap in a shorter ruler (a smaller reference), the same input reaches a higher tick mark. The tick number is meaningless until you know which ruler was used.

2. The Transfer Function — SLAU367P §34.2.1, Equation 13

TI's MSP430FR58xx/59xx family user's guide (SLAU367P) defines the ADC12_B conversion result in §34.2.1, Equation 13:

NADC  =  4095  ×  Vin − VR− VR+ − VR− 4095 = full-scale code for 12-bit mode; more generally FS = 2resolution − 1
  • Vin — the analog input voltage on the selected channel.
  • VR+ — the positive reference: the voltage that maps to full scale. Selected by ADC12VRSEL.
  • VR− — the negative reference: the voltage that maps to code 0. In Silmulator's model it is fixed at AVSS (0 V), so the equation simplifies to N = FS × Vin / VR+.
  • FS — the full-scale code: 4095 (12-bit), 1023 (10-bit), or 255 (8-bit), matching ADC12RES.

Worked example 1 — the probe case: 1.2 V input against the 1.2-V VREF

N = 4095 × (1.2 − 0) / (1.2 − 0)
  = 4095 × 1.0
  = 4095   # full scale — the input IS the reference

Worked example 2 — the same 1.2 V input against AVCC = 3.3 V

N = 4095 × (1.2 − 0) / (3.3 − 0)
  = 4095 × 0.36363…
  = 1489.09  →  int()  →  1489

Identical input, two references, codes of 4095 vs 1489. This exact pair is the audit probe (adc_ignores_reference) that exposed the bug: the old model returned 1489 regardless of the selected reference.

Worked example 3 — recovering volts from a code

Firmware and test scripts invert the transfer function to get volts back:

Vin ≈ N / FS × (VR+ − VR−) + VR−
     = 1489 / 4095 × 3.3
     = 1.19993 V   # ~1.2 V recovered — but ONLY if you divide by the SAME reference
⚠ Truncation, not rounding
Silmulator's nominal profile uses int(voltage / full_scale_v * max_code) — Python's int() truncates toward zero. An ideal result of 2047.5 becomes 2047, not 2048. Keep this in mind when predicting exact codes in the drill.

3. The Fix — What Commit 58b7e2d Actually Changed

Issue #18 came out of the MSP430 compliance audit (docs/audits/msp430-compliance-report.md). Two ADC families were NON_COMPLIANT for the same root cause: the model ignored the reference.

Before: a hardcoded 3.3 in the conversion path

# silmulator/silmulator/devices/msp430.py — BEFORE 58b7e2d
def _adc_ch_raw(self, cmd: ScpiCommand, ac: ADCChannel) -> str:
    return str(self.faults.adc_code(ac.value, 3.3, ac.resolution))
                                              # ↑ VR+ frozen at 3.3 V forever

And ADC:REFERENCE stored any string without complaint — ADC:REFERENCE BANANA succeeded, and the stored value was never read by the conversion code. Two independent defects: no validation and no effect.

After: VR+ is resolved from the selected reference at conversion time

# silmulator/silmulator/devices/msp430.py — AFTER 58b7e2d
def _adc_ch_raw(self, cmd: ScpiCommand, ac: ADCChannel) -> str:
    return str(self.faults.adc_code(ac.value, self._adc_reference_voltage(), ac.resolution))

def _adc_reference_voltage(self) -> float:
    """VR+ in volts for the selected ADC reference (SLAU367P §34.2.1 Eq. 13).

    VR- is AVSS (0 V) in this model — the simulator does not expose the
    VR- half of ADC12VRSEL's combinations, only which source drives VR+.
    """
    ref = self.adc[0].reference
    if ref == "AVCC":
        return self.clock.vcc          # reads CPU:VCC live — not a snapshot
    if ref == "VEREF":
        return self._veref_v           # the external VeREF+ pin voltage
    return ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V.get(ref, self.clock.vcc)  # REF_A outputs

The new module-level reference table

# REF_A's three internal reference outputs (SLAU367P §33.3.1, REFVSEL field).
# Bare "VREF" maps to REFVSEL's reset value (00b = 1.2 V).
ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V: Dict[str, float] = {
    "VREF":    1.2,
    "VREF1.2": 1.2,
    "VREF2.0": 2.0,
    "VREF2.5": 2.5,
}

# The fixed set ADC:REFERENCE accepts: AVCC (tracks CPU:VCC), REF_A's internal
# outputs, and VEREF (the external VeREF+ pin). Anything else has no
# ADC12VRSEL encoding and is rejected with -224.
VALID_ADC_REFERENCES = frozenset({"AVCC", "VEREF"} | set(ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V))

Validation in the SCPI handler

def _adc_ref(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
    if cmd.is_query:
        return self.adc[0].reference
    if cmd.params:
        ref = cmd.params[0].upper()
        if ref not in VALID_ADC_REFERENCES:
            raise ScpiError(-224, f"Illegal ADC reference: {ref}")
        if ref == "VEREF" and len(cmd.params) > 1:
            try:
                self._veref_v = float(cmd.params[1])
            except ValueError:
                raise ScpiError(-104, f"Invalid VEREF voltage: {cmd.params[1]}")
        for ch in self.adc.values():
            ch.reference = ref     # one reference for all channels (single-VR+ model)
    return ""

Tests flipped from expected-failure to passing

The two audit-derived tests dropped their @pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True) decorators — the code now does what SLAU367P says:

# tests/test_msp430_edge_cases.py — AFTER 58b7e2d (xfail decorators removed)
def test_reference_out_of_range_rejected(self, mcu):
    # SLAU367P §34.2.4 (ADC12VRSEL), §33 (REF_A): the reference is selected
    # from a fixed set (AVCC, 1.2/2.0/2.5-V REF, external) — not free-form.
    mcu.process("ADC:REFERENCE BANANA")
    assert errors(mcu) == 1

def test_raw_respects_selected_reference(self, mcu):
    # SLAU367P §34.2.1 Eq. 13: with VR+ = 1.2-V VREF, a 1.2-V input is full scale.
    mcu.process("ADC:REFERENCE VREF")
    mcu.inject_adc(0, 1.2)
    assert int(mcu.process("ADC:CHANNEL0:RAW?")) == 4095

Compliance moved from 19.8% → 22.8%: ADC:CHANNELn:RAW, ADC:CHn:RAW, and ADC:REFERENCE all flipped NON_COMPLIANT → COMPLIANT. (ADC:CONVERT now scales correctly too but stays NON_COMPLIANT for unrelated reasons: it runs without ADC12ENC and returns '0' for nonexistent channels.)

📌 One more detail: *RST
The new VeREF+ pin state self._veref_v is reset to 1.2 in the *RST handler, alongside all other peripheral state. Any new device state you add must be reset there too — that's the *RST contract.

4. Why References Are a Fixed Hardware Set (and -224 for Everything Else)

On a real MSP430FR5994 you cannot ask for a "1.8 V reference". The positive reference is selected by ADC12VRSEL — a 4-bit field in ADC12MCTLx (SLAU367P §34.2.4) whose encodings pick which physical voltage source drives VR+ and VR−. A register field with a finite set of encodings is the hardware truth the simulator must mirror.

The sources Silmulator models

SCPI tokenPhysical sourceVR+ value
AVCCThe analog supply railWhatever CPU:VCC is — read live at conversion time (default 3.3 V)
VREFREF_A internal reference, REFVSEL reset default (00b)1.2 V
VREF1.2REF_A internal reference, REFVSEL = 00b1.2 V
VREF2.0REF_A internal reference, REFVSEL = 01b2.0 V
VREF2.5REF_A internal reference, REFVSEL = 10b2.5 V
VEREFThe external VeREF+ pin (board-supplied)Whatever the test sets, e.g. ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.1 (default 1.2 V)

Three different kinds of reference source

  • AVCC — the supply itself. Cheap and always available, but it moves with the supply: brown-outs, battery droop, and regulator tolerance all show up as measurement error. Silmulator models this honestly: _adc_reference_voltage() reads self.clock.vcc at every conversion, so CPU:VCC 3.0 immediately rescales all subsequent conversions.
  • REF_A internal outputs — the FR5994's shared reference module (SLAU367P §33) generates precise 1.2 / 2.0 / 2.5 V from an internal bandgap, independent of the supply. This is what you use when the measurement must be in absolute volts.
  • VeREF+ — an external pin (SLASE54D Table 7-1) for boards that provide their own precision reference IC. Its voltage is whatever the board designer wired up — which is why Silmulator lets the test declare it: ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.048.

Why -224 specifically?

SCPI error -224, "Illegal parameter value" is the standard code for "the parameter is the right type but not one of the permitted values." The token BANANA (or 1.8, or 3V3) parses fine as a string — it just has no ADC12VRSEL encoding. Compare:

  • ADC:REFERENCE BANANA → -224 — not in the value set. The stored reference is left unchanged (still the AVCC default).
  • ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,notanumber → -104, "Data type error" — the reference token is valid, but the second parameter must be numeric.
  • ADC:RESOLUTION 9 → -224 — the sibling precedent: ADC12RES only encodes 8/10/12 bits, so 9 is rejected the same way.
💡 The design rule
When a SCPI parameter mirrors a hardware register field, the accepted value set is exactly the register's encodings — no more, no less. Free-form acceptance is how a simulator ends up blessing configurations that no silicon can express.

5. Full Scale, Clipping, and the LSB

Clipping: inputs above VR+ saturate

faults.adc_code() clamps the result to [0, max_code]. An input above the reference doesn't wrap or error — it pegs at full scale, exactly like real hardware:

# msp430_faults.py — nominal profile
max_code = (1 << resolution) - 1            # 4095 / 1023 / 255
code = int(voltage / full_scale_v * max_code)
return max(0, min(max_code, code))          # ← the clamp
Inject 2.5 V, reference VREF2.0:
N = 4095 × 2.5 / 2.0 = 5118.75  →  clamped  →  4095

Reading 4095 therefore means "at or above the reference" — the true voltage is unrecoverable. A real design leaves headroom; a SIL test can now verify that firmware treats 4095 as saturation, not as a valid measurement.

The LSB: what one code step is worth

One least-significant-bit step corresponds to (VR+ − VR−) / FS volts. The reference sets not just the range but the granularity:

ReferenceRange1 LSB (12-bit)Trade-off
VREF 1.2 V0 – 1.2 V≈ 293 µVFinest resolution, smallest range
VREF2.00 – 2.0 V≈ 488 µV
VREF2.50 – 2.5 V≈ 611 µV
AVCC 3.3 V0 – 3.3 V≈ 806 µVWidest range, coarsest steps, supply-dependent

This is why real firmware picks the smallest reference that still covers the signal: a 0–1 V sensor read against the 1.2-V VREF uses ~83% of the code space; against AVCC it uses only ~30%, throwing away 1.4 bits of effective resolution.

Resolution interacts the same way

ADC:RESOLUTION 8 changes FS to 255: injecting 3.3 V against AVCC 3.3 gives int(3.3/3.3 × 255) = 255 — the existing edge-case test. Reference and resolution are the two knobs of the same equation.

Ratiometric measurement: when AVCC is the right answer

If the sensor itself is powered from AVCC (a potentiometer, a resistive bridge), its output is already a fraction of AVCC. Converting it against AVCC makes the supply cancel out of the equation:

N = FS × k · AVCCAVCC = FS × k the code depends only on the sensor's fraction k — supply drift disappears

This is ratiometric measurement, and it is the reason "AVCC" exists as a reference choice at all. Silmulator's live clock.vcc read makes this testable: drop CPU:VCC and a ratiometric setup's code stays put, while an absolute-reference setup's code shifts.

6. Why This Matters for SIL Testing

Silmulator's purpose is to catch embedded-firmware bugs before hardware exists. The hardcoded 3.3 V broke that promise in a very specific way — it made the simulator agree with buggy firmware.

The bug class that was invisible

Consider firmware that configures the 2.5-V internal reference but converts codes to volts with the wrong constant:

/* firmware under test — BUG: reference is 2.5 V, math assumes 3.3 V */
float read_battery_volts(void) {
    select_reference(REF_2V5);            /* ADC12VRSEL = internal 2.5 V   */
    uint16_t raw = adc_convert(CH0);
    return raw / 4095.0f * 3.3f;          /* ← wrong unit of measure!      */
}
  • Old model: the simulated ADC also divided by 3.3, so raw/4095×3.3 round-tripped perfectly. The test passed. The bug shipped.
  • New model: injecting 1.5 V gives raw = int(1.5/2.5×4095) = 2457; the firmware computes 2457/4095×3.3 = 1.98 V. The SIL test's assertion ≈1.5 V fails — the mis-scaling is caught in simulation, exactly where it should be.

What else becomes testable

  • Reference-selection typos: firmware SCPI-driving a bad token now queues -224 instead of silently "working".
  • Supply-droop behaviour: CPU:VCC 3.0 rescales AVCC-referenced conversions live (1.2 V now reads 1638 instead of 1489) — brown-out compensation logic can be exercised.
  • Saturation handling: over-range inputs peg at 4095; firmware that treats 4095 as a real reading can be flagged.
  • Board-specific references: ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.048 models a precision external reference IC without any Python changes.
⚠ The general lesson
A simulator defect is worse than a missing feature. A missing feature fails loudly; a wrong constant makes the simulator and the buggy firmware wrong in the same direction, and every test between them passes. That is why the compliance audit probes behaviour (adc_ignores_reference) rather than trusting the command to exist.

7. Often Confused

ConfusionThe distinction
"Code 4095 means 3.3 V" Code 4095 means Vin ≥ VR+, whatever VR+ currently is. Under VREF it means ≥1.2 V; it can also mean the input is clipping far above the reference.
Reference voltage vs. supply voltage AVCC can serve as the reference, but they are distinct roles. The supply powers the chip; the reference defines the conversion's unit of measure. Only when ADC12VRSEL selects AVCC do they coincide — and then supply noise becomes measurement noise.
VREF vs VREF2.5 Bare VREF is not "some generic reference" — it maps to REFVSEL's reset value, 00b = 1.2 V. VREF1.2/2.0/2.5 select explicitly. Sending ADC:REFERENCE VREF and expecting 2.5-V scaling is a real trap.
ADC:CHANNELn:VALUE? vs :RAW? VALUE? returns the injected voltage in volts — test-harness introspection, no real-register counterpart (UNDOCUMENTED in the audit). RAW? is the modelled register read: a code, scaled by the reference. Only RAW goes through the transfer function.
-224 vs -104 -224 "Illegal parameter value": right type, not in the permitted set (ADC:REFERENCE BANANA). -104 "Data type error": wrong type entirely (ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,notanumber — the voltage must parse as a float).
Full-scale code vs full-scale voltage The full-scale code is fixed by resolution (4095 at 12-bit). The full-scale voltage is whatever reference you selected. Changing the reference moves the voltage that produces 4095; it never changes 4095 itself.

8. Quiz

Q1. With ADC:REFERENCE VREF2.0 selected and 1.0 V injected on channel 3, what does ADC:CHANNEL3:RAW? return in 12-bit mode?

  • 2047
  • 2048
  • 1241
  • 4095

Q2. A test sends ADC:REFERENCE 1.8 hoping for a 1.8-V reference. What happens?

  • The reference is set to 1.8 V and conversions scale accordingly
  • SCPI error -224 is queued and the previously selected reference is unchanged
  • SCPI error -104 is queued
  • It rounds to the nearest available reference (VREF2.0)

Q3. Why does _adc_reference_voltage() return self.clock.vcc for AVCC instead of the constant 3.3?

  • Pure style — 3.3 would work identically but constants are discouraged
  • AVCC is the live supply rail — CPU:VCC 3.0 must rescale subsequent conversions, as on real hardware
  • Because VEREF shares the same storage variable
  • Because the internal 1.2/2.0/2.5-V references also scale with VCC

Q4. With ADC:REFERENCE VREF2.0 selected, 2.5 V is injected. What does a 12-bit RAW read return, and why?

  • SCPI error -222 (data out of range)
  • 4095 — the ideal 5118 is clamped to full scale (clipping)
  • 1022 — the result wraps modulo 4096
  • 3103

Q5. Before commit 58b7e2d, a SIL test of firmware that selected the 2.5-V reference but converted codes with raw/4095×3.3 would pass. Why?

  • Simulator and firmware were both wrong by the same 3.3-V factor, so the errors cancelled
  • The old model rejected the 2.5-V reference so the firmware fell back to AVCC
  • The old model only supported 8-bit conversions
  • Voltage injection was broken before the commit

9. Scenarios — Check Your Understanding

Scenario A: Your board has a precision 2.048-V reference IC wired to the VeREF+ pin. Write the SCPI sequence to configure the simulated MSP430 to match, inject 1.024 V on channel 2, and predict the 12-bit RAW result. What error would you get if you typo'd the voltage as 2.O48 (letter O)?
Show answer 
ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.048     ← selects the external pin AND sets its voltage
ADC:CHANNEL2:INJECT 1.024
ADC:CHANNEL2:RAW?             → int(1.024 / 2.048 × 4095) = int(2047.5) = 2047

Exactly half the reference → half of full scale (truncated from 2047.5). With ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.O48, the token VEREF is valid but float("2.O48") raises ValueError, so the handler queues -104, "Invalid VEREF voltage: 2.O48" — a data-type error, not -224. The previously stored _veref_v is untouched. Also remember *RST resets _veref_v to 1.2, so the sequence must run after any reset.

Scenario B: A teammate reports "the ADC model is broken — I inject 1.2 V and RAW? returns 4095, but 1.2/3.3×4095 should be 1489." What do you check first, and what do you tell them?
Show answer

Check the selected reference: ADC:REFERENCE?. Almost certainly it returns VREF — someone (or a previous test, since the reference persists until *RST) selected the internal 1.2-V reference. Under VR+ = 1.2 V, a 1.2-V input is full scale: N = 4095 × 1.2/1.2 = 4095. This is the exact behaviour test_raw_respects_selected_reference asserts.

The teammate's formula smuggles in the assumption that 3.3 V is the unit of measure. The 1489 figure is only correct when AVCC (at its 3.3-V default) is selected. Their expectation is the pre-58b7e2d bug — the model used to behave that way, and it was NON_COMPLIANT. The fix: state expected codes as a function of the selected reference, or explicitly select ADC:REFERENCE AVCC at test setup.

Scenario C: You're writing a SIL test for battery-monitoring firmware that must keep working as the supply sags from 3.3 V to 3.0 V. The firmware measures a fixed 1.2-V bandgap-derived signal using AVCC as the reference and infers the supply from the code. Using only SCPI, how do you simulate the sag and what codes should the test expect at each supply level?
Show answer 
ADC:REFERENCE AVCC            ← unit of measure = the live supply
ADC:CHANNEL0:INJECT 1.2       ← the fixed signal being measured

CPU:VCC 3.3
ADC:CHANNEL0:RAW?             → int(1.2/3.3 × 4095) = 1489

CPU:VCC 3.0                   ← simulate the sag
ADC:CHANNEL0:RAW?             → int(1.2/3.0 × 4095) = 1638

Because _adc_reference_voltage() reads clock.vcc live, no re-arming is needed — the very next conversion uses the new supply. The trick the firmware exploits is the transfer function in reverse: the input is fixed, so a rising code means a falling reference. AVCC ≈ 4095 × 1.2 / N, so N = 1638 → AVCC ≈ 3.0 V. This measure-the-ruler-with-a-known-stick technique is only testable because the model stopped hardcoding 3.3 V.

ADC Reference Transfer Functions — Vocabulary

72

Eight terms behind the reference-aware ADC conversion. Each has a definition, a project example from the real code, a usage sentence, and a contrast with the term it's most often confused with.

73
74 75
76 reference voltage 77 full-scale code 78 transfer function 79 LSB voltage 80 ADC12VRSEL 81 REF_A 82 VeREF+ 83 ratiometric measurement 84
85 86 87
88

Reference voltage (VR+ / VR−)

89
the conversion's unit of measure
90
91
Definition
92
The voltage pair an ADC compares its input against: VR+ maps to the full-scale code, VR− maps to code 0. Every output code is a fraction of the span between them — the reference literally defines what one "unit" of the result means. Change the reference and the same physical input produces a different code.
93
Project example
94
In silmulator/devices/msp430.py, _adc_reference_voltage() resolves VR+ at conversion time — clock.vcc for AVCC, _veref_v for VEREF, or an ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V lookup for REF_A's outputs. VR− is fixed at AVSS (0 V) in this model. Before commit 58b7e2d, this function didn't exist and VR+ was a hardcoded 3.3.
95
Usage
96
"The RAW code looks huge because you left the 1.2-V reference voltage selected — 1.2 V in, 1.2 V reference, full scale out."
97
Contrast with: supply voltage
98
The supply (AVCC) powers the chip; the reference calibrates the measurement. They coincide only when AVCC is selected as the reference — and then supply drift becomes measurement drift, which is exactly what CPU:VCC 3.0 now lets a SIL test exercise.
99
100
101 102 103
104

Full-scale code (FS)

105
4095 · 1023 · 255
106
107
Definition
108
The maximum code an ADC can output: 2resolution − 1. It is produced when Vin ≥ VR+, so reading it means "at or above the reference" — possibly clipping — never a specific voltage.
109
Project example
110
msp430_faults.py computes max_code = (1 << resolution) - 1 and clamps with max(0, min(max_code, code)). The audit probe adc_ignores_reference asserts that 1.2 V against the 1.2-V VREF returns exactly 4095 — the input equals the reference, so the result is full scale.
111
Usage
112
"Inject 2.5 V against VREF2.0 and you'll read the full-scale code — the ideal 5118 clips to 4095."
113
Contrast with: full-scale voltage
114
The full-scale code is fixed by ADC:RESOLUTION (ADC12RES); the full-scale voltage is whatever reference is selected. Switching VREF2.5 → AVCC moves the voltage that produces 4095 from 2.5 V to 3.3 V, but 4095 itself never changes.
115
116
117 118 119
120

Transfer function

121
SLAU367P §34.2.1, Equation 13
122
123
Definition
124
The mapping from analog input to digital output code: NADC = FS × (Vin − VR−) / (VR+ − VR−), quantised and clamped. It makes explicit that an ADC code is a ratio of the reference span, not a voltage.
125
Project example
126
Implemented in FaultState.adc_code(): int(voltage / full_scale_v * max_code) with VR− = 0. Commit 58b7e2d's whole point was feeding the correct full_scale_v (the selected reference) into this function instead of the literal 3.3 — the CORNER profile then layers gain/offset/INL errors on top of the same ideal transfer curve.
127
Usage
128
"Work the transfer function forward to predict the code, and backward to recover volts — with the same reference both ways, or you get commit-58b7e2d's bug class."
129
Contrast with: calibration curve
130
The transfer function is the ideal, datasheet-defined mapping. A calibration curve characterises how a particular part deviates from it (gain, offset, INL — what the simulator's CORNER fault profile injects). You design against the transfer function; you correct against a calibration.
131
132
133 134 135
136

LSB voltage

137
(VR+ − VR−) / FS
138
139
Definition
140
The input-voltage width of one code step — the smallest voltage change the conversion can resolve. Set jointly by the reference span and the resolution: shrink the reference or raise the resolution, and each code is worth fewer microvolts.
141
Project example
142
With the references Silmulator now honours: 1.2 V / 4095 ≈ 293 µV per LSB under VREF, versus 3.3 V / 4095 ≈ 806 µV under default AVCC. The CORNER profile's INL spec is quoted in these units — a ±2.2-LSB bow in msp430_faults.py — which is only meaningful once you know the LSB's voltage value.
143
Usage
144
"Reading a 0–1 V sensor against AVCC wastes resolution — switch to VREF1.2 and your LSB voltage drops from 806 µV to 293 µV."
145
Contrast with: resolution (bit count)
146
Resolution is the number of steps (12-bit → 4096 of them); LSB voltage is how many volts each step spans. ADC:RESOLUTION changes the step count; ADC:REFERENCE changes the step size. Both knobs move the LSB voltage, only one moves the code range.
147
148
149 150 151
152

ADC12VRSEL

153
SLAU367P §34.2.4 — reference-select register field
154
155
Definition
156
The 4-bit field in the MSP430's ADC12MCTLx conversion-memory registers that selects which physical sources drive VR+ and VR−. Because it is a register field, the set of possible references is finite and fixed by silicon — there is no encoding for an arbitrary voltage.
157
Project example
158
VALID_ADC_REFERENCES = frozenset({"AVCC", "VEREF"} | set(ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V)) in msp430.py mirrors the VRSEL choices the model exposes. ADC:REFERENCE BANANA — or 1.8 — has no encoding, so _adc_ref raises ScpiError(-224, "Illegal ADC reference: …"), matching test_reference_out_of_range_rejected.
159
Usage
160
"The SCPI layer rejects free-form references because ADC12VRSEL is an enum in silicon, not a dial."
161
Contrast with: REFVSEL
162
ADC12VRSEL (in the ADC) picks which source feeds the reference inputs; REFVSEL (in REF_A, §33.3.1) picks which voltage — 1.2/2.0/2.5 V — the internal reference module generates. Silmulator folds both into one token: VREF2.5 effectively sets REFVSEL = 10b and points VRSEL at the internal reference.
163
164
165 166 167
168

REF_A

169
SLAU367P §33 — shared reference module
170
171
Definition
172
The FR5994's on-chip reference generator: a bandgap-derived module shared by the ADC and comparators that outputs a precise, supply-independent 1.2, 2.0, or 2.5 V (selected by REFVSEL, reset default 00b = 1.2 V).
173
Project example
174
Modelled by the ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V dict — {"VREF": 1.2, "VREF1.2": 1.2, "VREF2.0": 2.0, "VREF2.5": 2.5} — with bare VREF deliberately mapped to the REFVSEL reset value. The audit's MISSING list notes what is still absent: REFCTL0 semantics (REFON/REFOUT/REFGENRDY/REFBGRDY bits and the request/ready handshake).
175
Usage
176
"For an absolute battery-voltage reading, don't reference AVCC — take REF_A's 2.5-V output so supply sag can't skew the measurement."
177
Contrast with: AVCC as a reference
178
REF_A's outputs are fixed absolute voltages, immune to supply drift; AVCC tracks the supply (Silmulator reads clock.vcc live). Absolute measurements want REF_A; ratiometric sensors powered from the rail want AVCC.
179
180
181 182 183
184

VeREF+

185
SLASE54D Table 7-1 — external reference pin
186
187
Definition
188
The MSP430 pin through which a board supplies its own external positive reference — typically a precision reference IC (2.048 V, 4.096 V, …). Its voltage is a board-design decision, not a chip property, and it has no defined reset state after BOR.
189
Project example
190
Commit 58b7e2d added self._veref_v (default 1.2, restored by *RST) and the two-parameter SCPI form ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.1 — select the pin and declare what the board wires to it. A non-numeric voltage raises ScpiError(-104, …), pinned by test_veref_voltage_param_must_be_numeric.
191
Usage
192
"Our flight board has a 2.048-V reference IC on VeREF+, so the SIL setup sends ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.048 before any conversion."
193
Contrast with: VREF (internal)
194
VREF tokens select REF_A's on-chip outputs — fixed at 1.2/2.0/2.5 V, no configuration needed. VeREF+ is off-chip: any voltage the board provides, which is why it is the only reference whose value the test must declare (and the only one with a -104 failure mode).
195
196
197 198 199
200

Ratiometric measurement

201
when the supply cancels out
202
203
Definition
204
A measurement arrangement where the sensor's output and the ADC's reference derive from the same source, so the conversion measures the sensor's fraction and the source's absolute value cancels out of the transfer function: N = FS × (k·AVCC)/AVCC = FS × k.
205
Project example
206
Selecting ADC:REFERENCE AVCC makes _adc_reference_voltage() return self.clock.vcc live. A divider-style sensor modelled by injecting k × vcc reads the same code before and after CPU:VCC 3.0 — while an absolute injection like the fixed 1.2 V shifts from 1489 to 1638, which is how a SIL test tells the two arrangements apart.
207
Usage
208
"The potentiometer is powered from the rail, so keep the conversion ratiometric — referencing it to VREF2.5 would re-introduce the supply drift you're trying to cancel."
209
Contrast with: absolute measurement
210
Absolute measurement answers "how many volts?" and needs a supply-independent reference (REF_A or VeREF+). Ratiometric measurement answers "what fraction of the excitation?" and wants the supply as the reference. Choosing the wrong mode for the sensor type is a real firmware bug class the reference-aware model can now surface.

The mapping from analog input to digital output code: NADC = FS × (Vin − VR−) / (VR+ − VR−), quantised and clamped. It makes explicit that an ADC code is a ratio of the reference span, not a voltage.
Project example
Implemented in FaultState.adc_code(): int(voltage / full_scale_v * max_code) with VR− = 0. Commit 58b7e2d's whole point was feeding the correct full_scale_v (the selected reference) into this function instead of the literal 3.3 — the CORNER profile then layers gain/offset/INL errors on top of the same ideal transfer curve.
Usage
"Work the transfer function forward to predict the code, and backward to recover volts — with the same reference both ways, or you get commit-58b7e2d's bug class."
Contrast with: calibration curve
The transfer function is the ideal, datasheet-defined mapping. A calibration curve characterises how a particular part deviates from it (gain, offset, INL — what the simulator's CORNER fault profile injects). You design against the transfer function; you correct against a calibration.

LSB voltage

(VR+ − VR−) / FS
Definition
The input-voltage width of one code step — the smallest voltage change the conversion can resolve. Set jointly by the reference span and the resolution: shrink the reference or raise the resolution, and each code is worth fewer microvolts.
Project example
With the references Silmulator now honours: 1.2 V / 4095 ≈ 293 µV per LSB under VREF, versus 3.3 V / 4095 ≈ 806 µV under default AVCC. The CORNER profile's INL spec is quoted in these units — a ±2.2-LSB bow in msp430_faults.py — which is only meaningful once you know the LSB's voltage value.
Usage
"Reading a 0–1 V sensor against AVCC wastes resolution — switch to VREF1.2 and your LSB voltage drops from 806 µV to 293 µV."
Contrast with: resolution (bit count)
Resolution is the number of steps (12-bit → 4096 of them); LSB voltage is how many volts each step spans. ADC:RESOLUTION changes the step count; ADC:REFERENCE changes the step size. Both knobs move the LSB voltage, only one moves the code range.

ADC12VRSEL

SLAU367P §34.2.4 — reference-select register field
Definition
The 4-bit field in the MSP430's ADC12MCTLx conversion-memory registers that selects which physical sources drive VR+ and VR−. Because it is a register field, the set of possible references is finite and fixed by silicon — there is no encoding for an arbitrary voltage.
Project example
VALID_ADC_REFERENCES = frozenset({"AVCC", "VEREF"} | set(ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V)) in msp430.py mirrors the VRSEL choices the model exposes. ADC:REFERENCE BANANA — or 1.8 — has no encoding, so _adc_ref raises ScpiError(-224, "Illegal ADC reference: …"), matching test_reference_out_of_range_rejected.
Usage
"The SCPI layer rejects free-form references because ADC12VRSEL is an enum in silicon, not a dial."
Contrast with: REFVSEL
ADC12VRSEL (in the ADC) picks which source feeds the reference inputs; REFVSEL (in REF_A, §33.3.1) picks which voltage — 1.2/2.0/2.5 V — the internal reference module generates. Silmulator folds both into one token: VREF2.5 effectively sets REFVSEL = 10b and points VRSEL at the internal reference.

REF_A

SLAU367P §33 — shared reference module
Definition
The FR5994's on-chip reference generator: a bandgap-derived module shared by the ADC and comparators that outputs a precise, supply-independent 1.2, 2.0, or 2.5 V (selected by REFVSEL, reset default 00b = 1.2 V).
Project example
Modelled by the ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V dict — {"VREF": 1.2, "VREF1.2": 1.2, "VREF2.0": 2.0, "VREF2.5": 2.5} — with bare VREF deliberately mapped to the REFVSEL reset value. The audit's MISSING list notes what is still absent: REFCTL0 semantics (REFON/REFOUT/REFGENRDY/REFBGRDY bits and the request/ready handshake).
Usage
"For an absolute battery-voltage reading, don't reference AVCC — take REF_A's 2.5-V output so supply sag can't skew the measurement."
Contrast with: AVCC as a reference
REF_A's outputs are fixed absolute voltages, immune to supply drift; AVCC tracks the supply (Silmulator reads clock.vcc live). Absolute measurements want REF_A; ratiometric sensors powered from the rail want AVCC.

VeREF+

SLASE54D Table 7-1 — external reference pin
Definition
The MSP430 pin through which a board supplies its own external positive reference — typically a precision reference IC (2.048 V, 4.096 V, …). Its voltage is a board-design decision, not a chip property, and it has no defined reset state after BOR.
Project example
Commit 58b7e2d added self._veref_v (default 1.2, restored by *RST) and the two-parameter SCPI form ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.1 — select the pin and declare what the board wires to it. A non-numeric voltage raises ScpiError(-104, …), pinned by test_veref_voltage_param_must_be_numeric.
Usage
"Our flight board has a 2.048-V reference IC on VeREF+, so the SIL setup sends ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,2.048 before any conversion."
Contrast with: VREF (internal)
VREF tokens select REF_A's on-chip outputs — fixed at 1.2/2.0/2.5 V, no configuration needed. VeREF+ is off-chip: any voltage the board provides, which is why it is the only reference whose value the test must declare (and the only one with a -104 failure mode).

Ratiometric measurement

when the supply cancels out
Definition
A measurement arrangement where the sensor's output and the ADC's reference derive from the same source, so the conversion measures the sensor's fraction and the source's absolute value cancels out of the transfer function: N = FS × (k·AVCC)/AVCC = FS × k.
Project example
Selecting ADC:REFERENCE AVCC makes _adc_reference_voltage() return self.clock.vcc live. A divider-style sensor modelled by injecting k × vcc reads the same code before and after CPU:VCC 3.0 — while an absolute injection like the fixed 1.2 V shifts from 1489 to 1638, which is how a SIL test tells the two arrangements apart.
Usage
"The potentiometer is powered from the rail, so keep the conversion ratiometric — referencing it to VREF2.5 would re-introduce the supply drift you're trying to cancel."
Contrast with: absolute measurement
Absolute measurement answers "how many volts?" and needs a supply-independent reference (REF_A or VeREF+). Ratiometric measurement answers "what fraction of the excitation?" and wants the supply as the reference. Choosing the wrong mode for the sensor type is a real firmware bug class the reference-aware model can now surface.

Vocab 0009 · Silmulator · 2026-07-15 (overnight session, issue #18, commit 58b7e2d)
Companion lesson: ../lessons/0009-adc-reference-transfer-functions.html · Drill: ../drills/0009-adc-reference-transfer-functions.html

1. A Register Is a Container With a Physical Size

The core idea of this lesson: a hardware register is not a variable — it is a fixed number of flip-flops. TAxR, the Timer_A counter register (SLAU367P §25.2.1), is sixteen of them. Sixteen bits can represent exactly the integers 0 through 65535 (0xFFFF). The value 0x10000 does not "overflow" TAxR — it simply cannot exist in it, any more than a five-litre bucket can hold six litres.

Python, the language the simulator is written in, has no such limit. Its int is arbitrary-precision: ts.count = 0x12345 executes happily and stores 74565 in a "16-bit counter". This mismatch between the modeling language and the modeled hardware is the entire bug class of issue #19:

RegisterPhysical widthRepresentable valuesWhat the old model stored
TAxR (COUNT)16 bits0 … 0xFFFFAny Python int — 0x12345 verbatim
TAxCCRn (CC VALUE)16 bits0 … 0xFFFFAny Python int, unmasked
ID+TAIDEX (DIVIDER)2 + 3 bitsproducts of {1,2,4,8} × {1…8}, max /64/128 — a product no encoding produces
CAP (CC MODE)1 bitCOMPARE / CAPTURENothing — writes ignored, always read COMPARE

The audit probe that pinned the width defect could not be simpler:

# scripts/audit_msp430.py — BEFORE a20fbb1 (documenting the defect)
def probe_timer_count_over_16bit(dev: MSP430) -> bool:
    """TAxR is a 16-bit counter; the model stores 0x12345 verbatim."""
    dev.process("TIMERA0:COUNT 0x12345")
    return _errors(dev) == 0 and dev.timer_a[0].count == 0x12345
💡 The mental model
Every register write in a device model should pass through a question: "could these bits actually sit in that register?" If the answer is no, the model must do something other than store the value — because the silicon would. Width is the first, crudest filter; encodings (next section) are the finer one.

2. Encodings Bound Reachable Values — the ID × TAIDEX Worked Example

Width says a value fits; it does not say a value is reachable. The timer clock divider is the perfect example. There is no "divider register" holding a number like 64. There are two small fields (SLAU367P §25.2.1.1):

  • ID — 2 bits in TAxCTL, selecting a first-stage divide of 1, 2, 4, or 8
  • TAIDEX — 3 bits in TAxEX0, selecting a second-stage divide of 1 through 8

The effective divider is the product ID × TAIDEX. Enumerate every combination:

Why this matters: a Python int can hold 0x12345, but the 16-bit TAxR register it models cannot. Until commit a20fbb1 the MSP430 timer model accepted values, dividers, and register states that no silicon can reach — and every SIL test built on those states was silently void.

☐ 8. Misconceptions
☐ 9. Quiz

3. The Fix — What Commit a20fbb1 Actually Changed

Issue #19 covered four findings from the MSP430 compliance audit, all in the Timer_A/Timer_B model, all instances of "the model accepts states silicon can't hold". The commit touched one dataclass and four handlers in silmulator/devices/msp430.py.

Width enforcement on the counter (TAxR)

def _timer_count(self, cmd: ScpiCommand, ts: TimerState) -> str:
    """TAxR/TBxR count register (SLAU367P §25.2.1/§26.2.1): 16-bit counter."""
    if cmd.is_query:
        return str(ts.count)
    if cmd.params:
        ts.count = int(cmd.params[0], 0)              # BEFORE — any int stored
        v = int(cmd.params[0], 0)
        if not 0 <= v <= 0xFFFF:
            raise ScpiError(-222, "Timer count out of range (0-0xFFFF)")
        ts.count = v
    return ""

The identical guard went into _timer_cc_val for the TAxCCRn compare registers ("CCR value out of range (0-0xFFFF)"). Note the check is two-sided: -1 is just as unrepresentable in an unsigned 16-bit register as 0x10000.

The CAP bit becomes real stored state

def _timer_cc_mode(self, cmd: ScpiCommand, ts: TimerState, cc: int) -> str:
    """CAP bit (SLAU367P §25.2.4/§26.2.4): COMPARE or CAPTURE mode.

    Stored state only — no waveform capture is simulated (no edge inputs
    latch TAxCCRn) since time does not pass in this simulation.
    """
    VALID = {"COMPARE", "CAPTURE"}
    if cmd.is_query:
        return "COMPARE"                       # BEFORE — writes ignored, constant read
        return ts.cc_mode.get(cc, "COMPARE")
    if cmd.params:
        v = cmd.params[0].upper()
        if v not in VALID:
            raise ScpiError(-224, f"Illegal CC mode: {v}")
        ts.cc_mode[cc] = v
    return ""

Backing it, TimerState gained a per-CC-unit dict — and lost a field (next section):

# TimerState dataclass
period: int = 0xFFFF                                    # BEFORE — an independent store
capture_compare: Dict[int, int] = field(default_factory=lambda: {0: 0, 1: 0, 2: 0, 3: 0})
cc_mode: Dict[int, str] = field(default_factory=lambda: {0: "COMPARE", 1: "COMPARE", 2: "COMPARE", 3: "COMPARE"})

Four strict xfails flipped to regression guards

Exactly as in issue #18, the tests documenting these defects carried @pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True). The commit deleted four decorators, promoting the tests:

# tests/test_msp430_edge_cases.py — now plain passing tests
def test_divider_128_rejected(self, mcu):
    # SLAU367P §25.2.1.1: no ID x TAIDEX combination produces /128.
    mcu.process("TIMERA0:CLOCK:DIVIDER 128")
    assert errors(mcu) == 1

def test_count_over_16bit_rejected_or_masked(self, mcu):
    # SLAU367P §25.2.1: a 16-bit counter cannot hold 0x10000.
    mcu.process("TIMERA0:COUNT 0x10000")
    assert errors(mcu) == 1 or mcu.timer_a[0].count <= 0xFFFF

def test_capture_mode_settable(self, mcu):
    # SLAU367P §25.2.4 (CAP bit): each CC unit supports capture mode.
    mcu.process("TIMERA0:CC1:MODE CAPTURE")
    assert mcu.process("TIMERA0:CC1:MODE?") == "CAPTURE"

def test_period_is_ccr0_in_up_mode(self, mcu):
    # SLAU367P §25.2.3.1: in up mode the period register IS TAxCCR0.
    mcu.process("TIMERA0:MODE UP")
    mcu.process("TIMERA0:PERIOD 1000")
    assert int(mcu.process("TIMERA0:CC0:VALUE?")) == 1000

The audit rescored: Timer_A/B COUNT moved ACCEPTS_INVALID → PARTIAL (width enforced; the counter still never advances), CLOCK:DIVIDER and PERIOD → COMPLIANT, CC:MODE NON_COMPLIANT → PARTIAL. The vendor-doc diff moved from 13 MATCH / 5 CONFLICT to 17 MATCH / 1 CONFLICT.

4. Reject vs Mask — the Policy Choice for Over-Width Writes

When a write doesn't fit the register, a simulator has three options. Only one is wrong:

PolicyBehaviour on COUNT 0x12345Verdict
Store verbatimcount = 74565 — a state no TAxR can hold❌ The bug. Every later read is fiction.
Mask (truncate to width)count = 0x12345 & 0xFFFF = 0x2345✓ Hardware-faithful for bus writes
Reject (queue an error)count unchanged, SCPI error -222 queued✓ Hardware-faithful and loud — this repo's choice

Both mask and reject keep the state space honest, and the flipped test deliberately accepts either policy — assert errors(mcu) == 1 or mcu.timer_a[0].count <= 0xFFFF — because both are defensible readings of the silicon. Why did this repo pick reject with -222?

  • The write is already a firmware bug. On the real part a 16-bit bus write physically can't carry 0x12345; C code that computes an over-width timer value has truncated it (or invoked implementation-defined behaviour) before the store. A SCPI parameter is wider than a bus, so the simulator sees the un-truncated intent — and an error queue entry points a finger at it. Masking would reproduce the hardware result while hiding the mistake.
  • Silent masking mimics the silent hardware failure. A masked 0x1F400 → 0xF400 "works" and produces a period ~4× off. The whole point of SIL is to catch that in simulation with a diagnosis, not to faithfully reproduce the confusion.
  • It matches the codebase's precedent — ADC:RESOLUTION 9, ADC:REFERENCE BANANA, illegal GPIO pins: this model consistently validates and rejects rather than coercing.

-222 vs -224: two flavours of rejection

Issue #19's handlers use both standard SCPI codes, and the distinction is worth internalising:

CodeMeaningUsed whenExample
-222Data out of rangeNumeric parameter outside the register's representable rangeCOUNT 0x10000, CC1:VALUE 70000, COUNT -1
-224Illegal parameter valueValue not in a finite encoding set (membership test)DIVIDER 128, CC1:MODE BANANA, MODE SIDEWAYS
💡 The design rule
A range violation (the value type is right, the magnitude isn't) gets -222. A set-membership violation (the value has no encoding at all) gets -224. The divider is -224 even though 128 is numeric, because the divider is an enumerated set of reachable products, not a continuous range.

    capture_compare: Dict[int, int]    # store #2 — TIMERn:CC0:VALUE reads/writes [0]

def _timer_period(self, cmd, ts):
    if cmd.is_query: return str(ts.period)
    if cmd.params:   ts.period = int(cmd.params[0], 0)

Watch it diverge:

TIMERA0:MODE UP
TIMERA0:PERIOD 1000        # store #1 ← 1000
TIMERA0:CC0:VALUE?         # → 0        (store #2 untouched!)
TIMERA0:CC0:VALUE 500      # store #2 ← 500
TIMERA0:PERIOD?            # → 1000     (store #1 unaware)

On real silicon both queries read the same flip-flops — the answers would be 1000 and then 500. The simulator held two contradictory truths at once, a state the hardware cannot even represent. Any SIL test that mixed the two names (set the period via one, verify PWM duty via the other) was comparing apples to a hallucination.

The fix: delegate, don't duplicate

# AFTER a20fbb1 — one store, two names
def _timer_period(self, cmd: ScpiCommand, ts: TimerState) -> str:
    """PERIOD — alias of TAxCCR0/TBxCCR0 (SLAU367P §25.2.3.1/§26.2.3.1).

    In up mode the period register IS CCR0; hardware has one register, so
    PERIOD is not an independent store — it reads/writes capture_compare[0].
    """
    return self._timer_cc_val(cmd, ts, 0)

The period field was deleted, not synchronised. That is the important design move: keeping two stores and copying between them ("shadow-register style") invites the next divergence bug the moment someone adds a third write path. One store per hardware register means the alias cannot drift — and PERIOD inherits CCR0's 16-bit -222 width guard for free.

⚠ A visible side effect: the reset value changed
The old independent period defaulted to 0xFFFF; TAxCCR0 — like the real register after a reset — defaults to 0. So after *RST, TIMERA0:PERIOD? now answers 0, not 65535. Correctness sometimes changes answers tests were relying on; that is the point of pinning behaviour to the vendor doc rather than to the model's history.

6. Stored-State-Only Modeling — the CAP Bit and the Absence of Time

Silmulator's devices are state machines without a clock: state changes only when a SCPI command changes it. Time does not pass. The counter never increments; interrupts never fire on their own; no waveform edge ever arrives. This is a deliberate architecture, and the CAP-bit fix shows exactly how to model honestly inside it.

What the CAP bit is

Each capture/compare unit has a CAP bit (SLAU367P §25.2.4): 0 = compare mode (CCRn holds a value you wrote; the timer compares its count against it — PWM, periodic interrupts), 1 = capture mode (an input edge latches the current count into CCRn — timestamping, pulse-width measurement).

What the model does — and pointedly does not — simulate

  • Stored: the CAP bit itself. TIMERA0:CC1:MODE CAPTURE persists in ts.cc_mode[1] and reads back CAPTURE. Invalid tokens are rejected with -224. Configuration round-trips faithfully.
  • Not simulated: the capture event machinery — CM edge select, CCIS input select, SCS synchronisation, and the latch of TAxR into TAxCCRn. There are no edges because there is no time.

When a behaviour needs time and the simulator has none, split it: model the configuration state fully (store, validate, read back, reset in *RST), and document the dynamic half as out of scope in the docstring and the audit. 7. Why This Matters for SIL Testing

Accepting an unreachable state doesn't crash anything. That is exactly what makes it dangerous: every SIL result computed downstream of an impossible state is silently void. The test ran, the assertions passed, and none of it says anything about real hardware, because the simulated device was in a configuration no silicon can occupy.

Worked example: the /128 divider

Firmware wants a slow tick from SMCLK for a long-interval poll, and a developer writes the driver with a /128 divide:

/* firmware under test — BUG: no ID×TAIDEX product reaches /128 */
timer_set_divider(TIMER_A0, 128);          /* driver silently clamps? wraps? …  */
timer_set_period_ms(TIMER_A0, 20);         /* period math assumes /128 tick     */
  • Old model: TIMERA0:CLOCK:DIVIDER 128 stored 128; every derived figure (tick frequency, period counts) computed on a clock no MSP430 can produce. The SIL test validated timing math for imaginary hardware — and passed.
  • New model: the write queues -224 "Illegal divider: 128" and the divider stays put. The test fails at the configuration step, which is where the firmware bug actually lives: the driver's divider table needs entries the hardware has (e.g. /64 with doubled period counts).

Worked example: the over-width period

At a 1-MHz tick, a 200-ms period needs 200,000 counts. 0x30D40 does not fit in TAxCCR0:

  • Old model: TIMERA0:PERIOD 200000 stored verbatim. A test asserting PERIOD? == 200000 passed. On the bench, the register truncates to 0x0D40 (3392 counts ≈ 3.4 ms) — a ~59× faster interrupt storm the SIL run never hinted at.
  • New model: -222 "CCR value out of range (0-0xFFFF)". The firmware must be restructured (bigger divider, or count rollovers in software) — a real design constraint surfaced in simulation, before the bench.

The audit's scoring philosophy, restated

Notice that fixing these did not require simulating more behaviour. COUNT is still a static register; capture still never latches. The verdicts improved because the model stopped lying about the state space. In this codebase's terms:

  • ACCEPTS_INVALID is a worse defect than MISSING — a missing command fails loudly; an accepted-invalid state fails silently, downstream, on the bench.
  • The vendor-doc diff (test_vendor_doc_diff.py) flipped its pinned expectation from "this CONFLICT exists" to "this command is a MATCH" — the diff report is itself regression-tested, so the gap can't quietly reopen.
⚠ The general lesson
A device simulator's first duty is not to do everything the hardware does — it is to refuse everything the hardware can't. Reachability guards are cheap (a range check, a frozen set, a delegated store) and they convert "silently void SIL results" into "loud, diagnosable failures at the exact line that's wrong".

8. Often Confused

ConfusionThe distinction
Width violation vs encoding violation Width: the number needs more bits than the register has (0x10000 in TAxR → -222). Encoding: the number fits, but no field combination produces it (/128 in ID×TAIDEX → -224). The divider bug was an encoding bug — 128 fits in 16 bits just fine.
"Reject" vs "mask" vs "store verbatim" Reject and mask are both hardware-honest policies (the flipped test accepts either); this repo rejects with -222 to make the firmware bug loud. Store-verbatim is the only wrong answer — it manufactures unreachable state.
Unreachable vs merely un-modeled values /128 is unreachable in silicon — accepting it is a compliance bug. /48 IS reachable (8×6) but outside the model's power-of-two VALID set — rejecting it is a documented simplification. Both are rejected, for opposite reasons; only one was an audit finding.
Register alias vs shadow register An alias is one store with two names (PERIOD → capture_compare[0]; nothing to synchronise). A shadow/latch is two real stores with a defined hand-off (Timer_B's TBxCLn compare latches — still unmodeled). The old PERIOD was an accidental shadow with no hand-off: the worst of both.
CAP bit (configuration) vs capture event (behaviour) The bit is stored state the model now round-trips; the event (edge latches TAxR into CCRn) needs time, which the simulation doesn't have. "Mode reads back CAPTURE" does not mean a capture will ever happen.
PERIOD? returning 0 after reset: bug or fix? Fix. The old 0xFFFF default belonged to the phantom second store. TAxCCR0 resets to 0, so the alias reads 0 — matching silicon. Tests that assumed 65535 were pinned to the model, not the part.
-222 vs -224 -222 "Data out of range": numeric magnitude outside the representable range (COUNT/CCR width guards). -224 "Illegal parameter value": not a member of a finite value set (DIVIDER 128, CC1:MODE BANANA). Range check vs membership check.

  • The vendor-doc diff (test_vendor_doc_diff.py) flipped its pinned expectation from "this CONFLICT exists" to "this command is a MATCH" — the diff report is itself regression-tested, so the gap can't quietly reopen.

+ A device simulator's first duty is not to do everything the hardware does — it is to refuse everything the hardware can't. Reachability guards are cheap (a range check, a frozen set, a delegated store) and they convert "silently void SIL results" into "loud, diagnosable failures at the exact line that's wrong".

+ Width: the number needs more bits than the register has (0x10000 in TAxR → -222). Encoding: the number fits, but no field combination produces it (/128 in ID×TAIDEX → -224). The divider bug was an encoding bug — 128 fits in 16 bits just fine.

+ Reject and mask are both hardware-honest policies (the flipped test accepts either); this repo rejects with -222 to make the firmware bug loud. Store-verbatim is the only wrong answer — it manufactures unreachable state.

+ /128 is unreachable in silicon — accepting it is a compliance bug. /48 IS reachable (8×6) but outside the model's power-of-two VALID set — rejecting it is a documented simplification. Both are rejected, for opposite reasons; only one was an audit finding.

+ An alias is one store with two names (PERIOD → capture_compare[0]; nothing to synchronise). A shadow/latch is two real stores with a defined hand-off (Timer_B's TBxCLn compare latches — still unmodeled). The old PERIOD was an accidental shadow with no hand-off: the worst of both.

+ The bit is stored state the model now round-trips; the event (edge latches TAxR into CCRn) needs time, which the simulation doesn't have. "Mode reads back CAPTURE" does not mean a capture will ever happen.
+ PERIOD? returning 0 after reset: bug or fix?
+ Fix. The old 0xFFFF default belonged to the phantom second store. TAxCCR0 resets to 0, so the alias reads 0 — matching silicon. Tests that assumed 65535 were pinned to the model, not the part.

+ -222 "Data out of range": numeric magnitude outside the representable range (COUNT/CCR width guards). -224 "Illegal parameter value": not a member of a finite value set (DIVIDER 128, CC1:MODE BANANA). Range check vs membership check.

9. Quiz

Q1. A test sends TIMERA0:COUNT 0x10000. What happens after commit a20fbb1?

  • SCPI error -222 is queued and the stored count is unchanged
  • The value is masked to 0x0000 and stored
  • 0x10000 is stored — Python ints have no width limit
  • SCPI error -224 is queued

Q2. Why is TIMERA0:CLOCK:DIVIDER 128 rejected when 128 fits easily in 16 bits?

  • The divider is the product ID × TAIDEX, whose maximum is 8 × 8 = 64 — no encoding reaches 128
  • The divider register is only 7 bits wide
  • 128 is rejected only because the model arbitrarily stops at 64
  • Dividing SMCLK by 128 would produce a frequency below the timer's minimum

Q3. After TIMERA0:MODE UP and TIMERA0:PERIOD 1000, what does TIMERA0:CC0:VALUE? return, and why?

  • 1000 — PERIOD is an alias that reads and writes capture_compare[0] directly
  • 0 — PERIOD and CC0 are independent registers
  • 1000 — the handler copies the period value into CCR0 after each write
  • SCPI error -221 — PERIOD is only writable in up mode

Q4. TIMERA0:CC1:MODE CAPTURE succeeds and reads back CAPTURE. What will the model do when firmware later polls TIMERA0:CC1:VALUE? for a captured timestamp?

  • It returns the last value written to CCR1 — no capture event ever latches the count, because time does not pass
  • It returns the current count, latched at the moment of the next simulated edge
  • SCPI error -230 — the register is owned by the capture machinery
  • The mode silently reverts to COMPARE on the first CCR1 read

Q5. Why is a model that accepts an unreachable state considered worse than a model that is missing a command entirely?

  • A missing command fails loudly at the call site; an accepted unreachable state silently voids every result computed after it
  • They are equally bad — both are non-compliances
  • Unreachable states waste memory and slow the simulation
  • Unreachable states eventually crash the Python process

10. Scenarios — Check Your Understanding

Scenario A: Firmware needs a 100-ms period from a 1-MHz SMCLK. A teammate proposes TIMERA0:CLOCK:DIVIDER 1 + TIMERA0:PERIOD 100000. Predict exactly what the simulator does, then fix the configuration using only reachable states.
Show answer

The divider write succeeds (1 is in the valid set), but PERIOD 100000 hits the CCR0 width guard: 100000 > 0xFFFF (65535), so the model queues -222 "CCR value out of range (0-0xFFFF)" and CCR0 is unchanged. Before a20fbb1 it would have stored 100000 and the test would have validated an impossible timer.

Fix: buy back range with the prescaler. TIMERA0:CLOCK:DIVIDER 2 gives a 500-kHz tick, so 100 ms = 50,000 counts — fits: TIMERA0:PERIOD 50000. (Divider 4 and 25,000 counts also works, with coarser resolution.) The general recipe: counts = t × fclk / divider; pick the smallest reachable divider that brings counts ≤ 65535.

Scenario B: A PWM SIL test written before a20fbb1 did TIMERA0:PERIOD 1000, TIMERA0:CC1:VALUE 250, then asserted duty = CC1 / CC0 = 25% by querying both CC registers. It passed then and passes now — but for different reasons. What changed underneath it, and what sibling test broke?
Show answer

Before: CC0:VALUE? read the capture_compare[0] store, which the PERIOD write never touched — it read 0, and duty was 250/0: the test only "passed" if it queried PERIOD? instead of CC0 (two stores, two truths). After: PERIOD delegates to capture_compare[0], so CC0:VALUE? genuinely returns 1000 and the duty math is grounded in one store, as on silicon.

The sibling that breaks: anything pinned to the old defaults or the double store — e.g. a test asserting PERIOD? returns 65535 after *RST (the deleted field's 0xFFFF default; the alias now reads CCR0's reset value, 0), or one asserting PERIOD and CC0 can hold different values. Those tests were pinned to the model's fiction, not the part.

Scenario C: You're adding a new device command DAC:GAIN mirroring a 2-bit register field with encodings ×1, ×2, ×4, ×8. Using issue #19's patterns, write the handler skeleton: what do you validate, which SCPI errors do you use, and what belongs in the docstring?
Show answer 
def _dac_gain(self, cmd: ScpiCommand, ds: DACState) -> str:
    """DAC gain (vendor doc §x.y): 2-bit field, encodings x1/x2/x4/x8."""
    VALID = {1, 2, 4, 8}                # the reachable set — nothing else
    if cmd.is_query:
        return str(ds.gain)
    if cmd.params:
        v = int(cmd.params[0])
        if v not in VALID:
            raise ScpiError(-224, f"Illegal DAC gain: {v}")
        ds.gain = v
    return ""

Checklist from issue #19: (1) the accepted set is exactly the register's encodings — a 2-bit field reaches at most 4 values, so ×3 or ×16 must be rejected; (2) -224 because this is set membership, not a numeric range (a raw 16-bit level register would use a 0 ≤ v ≤ 0xFFFF guard with -222); (3) reject before assignment so state never holds an illegal value; (4) docstring cites the vendor-doc section and states any stored-state-only limitation; (5) the field's default must be restored by *RST (dataclass default), and a probe/test should pin the rejection.

input.new_string: // ─── CHANNEL: width ─────────────────────────────────────────── {id:'w1',ch:'width',type:'w', q:'TAxR is described as "a 16-bit counter". Derive its representable value range, explain why 0xFFFF is accepted but 0x10000 is not, and state what the model does for each write after commit a20fbb1.', c:[{l:'16 bits → 0 … 2^16 − 1 = 65535 (0xFFFF)',t:['65535','0xffff','2^16','2**16','16 bits']}, {l:'0x10000 needs a 17th bit — unrepresentable',t:['0x10000','17','65536','does not fit','cannot hold','unrepresentable']}, {l:'0xFFFF stored and reads back; 0x10000 → ScpiError -222',t:['-222','rejected','out of range','stored']}, {l:'state unchanged on rejection',t:['unchanged','previous','not stored','untouched','before the assignment']}], m:`Sixteen flip-flops represent exactly 2^16 = 65536 states: the integers 0 through 65535 (0xFFFF). 0xFFFF is the all-ones pattern — the last representable value — so TIMERA0:COUNT 0xFFFF stores and reads back 65535 (test_count_16bit_maximum pins this, with zero errors). 0x10000 is 65536: it needs a seventeenth bit that the register does not have. It is not "too big and wraps" — in the register it simply has no representation. After a20fbb1, _timer_count guards the write: if not 0 <= v <= 0xFFFF, it raises ScpiError(-222, "Timer count out of range (0-0xFFFF)") BEFORE assignment, so ts.count keeps its previous value. lines: // QUESTION BANK  (24 questions — grounded in commit a20fbb1)

+ q:'TAxR is described as "a 16-bit counter". Derive its representable value range, explain why 0xFFFF is accepted but 0x10000 is not, and state what the model does for each write after commit a20fbb1.',
+    {l:'0x10000 needs a 17th bit — unrepresentable',t:['0x10000','17','65536','does not fit','cannot hold','unrepresentable']},
+    {l:'0xFFFF stored and reads back; 0x10000 → ScpiError -222',t:['-222','rejected','out of range','stored']},
+    {l:'state unchanged on rejection',t:['unchanged','previous','not stored','untouched','before the assignment']}],

+ m:`Sixteen flip-flops represent exactly 2^16 = 65536 states: the integers 0 through 65535 (0xFFFF). 0xFFFF is the all-ones pattern — the last representable value — so TIMERA0:COUNT 0xFFFF stores and reads back 65535 (test_count_16bit_maximum pins this, with zero errors).
+0x10000 is 65536: it needs a seventeenth bit that the register does not have. It is not "too big and wraps" — in the register it simply has no representation.

+After a20fbb1, _timer_count guards the write: if not 0 <= v <= 0xFFFF, it raises ScpiError(-222, "Timer count out of range (0-0xFFFF)") BEFORE assignment, so ts.count keeps its previous value. Before the fix, the model stored 0x12345-style values verbatim — an unreachable state that voided any SIL result computed from it.`
+ q:'What does TIMERA0:COUNT -1 do after commit a20fbb1?',
+ raise ScpiError(-222, "Timer count out of range (0-0xFFFF)")`,

+  {t:'Queues -222 — the guard is two-sided, and an unsigned 16-bit register cannot represent a negative value',c:true, w:'Correct. The chained comparison 0 <= v <= 0xFFFF rejects both directions of unrepresentability: too big (0x10000) and negative (-1). TAxR holds bit patterns 0…65535; there is no sign bit.'},

+  {t:'Stores 0xFFFF — negative values wrap two\'s-complement style',c:false,w:'Two\'s-complement wrapping is a CPU-arithmetic convention, not a register-write policy. The model rejects rather than reinterpreting the bits.'},

+  {t:'Stores -1 — Python ints are signed',c:false,w:'Python would happily hold -1, which is exactly why the explicit guard exists: the modeling language is wider than the modeled register in both directions.'},

+  {t:'Queues -224 — negative numbers are not in the valid set',c:false,w:'-224 is for finite-set membership violations (DIVIDER 128). A numeric magnitude/sign outside the representable range is -222, Data out of range.'},
+ q:'Which of these writes succeeds with no error after a20fbb1?',

+  {t:'TIMERA0:CC0:VALUE 0xFFFF',c:true, w:'Correct. 0xFFFF = 65535 is the top of the representable range — a boundary value, not an overflow. test_capture_compare_boundary_value pins that it stores and reads back exactly.'},
+  {t:'TIMERA0:CC1:VALUE 70000',c:false,w:'70000 > 65535 → ScpiError(-222, "CCR value out of range (0-0xFFFF)"). CCRn got the same width guard as COUNT.'},
+  {t:'TIMERA0:COUNT 0x12345',c:false,w:'0x12345 = 74565 needs 17 bits. This is the exact value the audit probe used to demonstrate the old verbatim-store defect; it is now rejected with -222.'},
+  {t:'TIMERA0:CLOCK:DIVIDER 128',c:false,w:'128 fits in 16 bits but no ID×TAIDEX encoding produces it — rejected with -224. Width is fine; reachability is not.'},

+ q:'A masking policy would compute count = value & 0xFFFF. Apply it to 0x12345 and to 0x10000, then explain why the flipped test test_count_over_16bit_rejected_or_masked accepts masking even though this repo rejects instead.',
+    {l:'mask keeps only the low 16 bits — what a 16-bit bus write would land',t:['low 16','lower 16','truncat','bus','& 0xffff']},
+    {l:'both policies keep state representable; test asserts errors==1 OR count<=0xFFFF',t:['either','or count','representable','both','defensible','<= 0xffff']}],
+ m:`Masking keeps only the low 16 bits:
+- 0x10000 & 0xFFFF = 0x0000 — all the value was in the 17th bit.

+That is what real silicon effectively does for a bus write: only 16 wires arrive, so only 16 bits land. The test asserts "errors(mcu) == 1 or mcu.timer_a[0].count <= 0xFFFF" because BOTH policies keep the state space honest — either the write is refused (reject) or the stored value is representable (mask). What the test forbids is the third option: storing the over-width value verbatim.

+This repo chose reject (-222) over mask because the un-truncated value arriving at the SCPI layer is evidence of a firmware/test bug, and a queued error diagnoses it at the offending line, whereas masking would silently reproduce the confusing hardware outcome.`
+ q:'At a 1-MHz timer tick, firmware wants a 200-ms period and computes 200000 counts. What happens on TIMERA0:PERIOD 200000, and what is the correct engineering fix?',

+  {t:'-222 queued (PERIOD inherits CCR0\'s 16-bit guard); fix by raising the clock divider so the count fits, e.g. /4 → 50000 counts',c:true, w:'Correct. PERIOD delegates to _timer_cc_val(cmd, ts, 0), so the CCR width guard applies: 200000 > 65535 → -222. The design fix is to trade resolution for range via the prescaler: at /4 the tick is 250 kHz and 200 ms = 50000 counts ≤ 0xFFFF.'},

+  {t:'The period is stored; PERIOD is a logical setting, not a register',c:false,w:'Since a20fbb1, PERIOD IS the TAxCCR0 register (one store, two names) — so it is exactly as wide as CCR0: 16 bits.'},
+  {t:'-224 queued — 200000 is not in the period\'s valid set',c:false,w:'The period is a numeric range (0…0xFFFF), not an enumerated set, so the range-violation code -222 applies.'},
+  {t:'The value is split across CCR0 and CCR1 automatically',c:false,w:'No such widening exists in the timer. Long intervals need a bigger divider or software rollover counting.'},

input.new_string: // ─── CHANNEL: enc ───────────────────────────────────────────── {id:'e1',ch:'enc',type:'w', q:'Enumerate the reachable timer clock dividers from the ID and TAIDEX fields (SLAU367P §25.2.1.1): give the two field ranges, the size of the reachable set, the maximum, and two examples of values below 64 that are NOT reachable.', c:[{l:'ID ∈ {1,2,4,8} (2 bits); TAIDEX ∈ {1…8} (3 bits)',t:['1,2,4,8','{1, 2, 4, 8}','1-8','1…8','1 to 8','taidex']}, {l:'divider = ID × TAIDEX product',t:['product','×','multipl','x taidex']}, {l:'20 distinct reachable values; max 8×8 = 64',t:['20','64','8×8','8 x 8','8*8']}, {l:'unreachable below 64: e.g. 9, 11, 13, 15, 17…',t:['9','11','13','15','17']}], m:`ID is a 2-bit field in TAxCTL dividing by 1, 2, 4, or 8. TAIDEX is a 3-bit field in TAxEX0 dividing by 1 through 8. The effective divider is the product ID × TAIDEX. Enumerating all 4 × 8 = 32 combinations and collapsing duplicates gives 20 distinct values: {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,10,12,14,16,20,24,28,32,40,48,56,64}. The maximum is 8 × 8 = 64. Not every integer below 64 is reachable: 9, 11, 13, 15, 17 (and any value with a prime factor other than 2, 3, 5, 7 arranged outside {1,2,4,8}×{1..8}) has no factorisation into the two fields. And /128 would need a 16 in one field — no 2-bit or 3-bit encoding provides one, which is why the old model's acceptance of 128 was a compliance bug.` }, {id:'e2',ch:'enc',type:'mc', q:'What does the fixed model do with TIMERA0:CLOCK:DIVIDER 128, per the rewritten audit probe?', snip:`# scripts/audit_msp430.py — AFTER a20fbb1 def probe_timer_divider_128(dev): """/128 is rejected — no ID×TAIDEX combination produces it (§25.2.1.1).""" dev.process("TIMERA0:CLOCK:DIVIDER 128") return _errors(dev) == 1 and dev.timer_a[0].clock_divider == 1`, opts:[ {t:'One error is queued (-224 "Illegal divider: 128") and the divider stays at its previous value — the reset default 1 in the probe',c:true, w:'Correct. 128 fails the VALID = {1,2,4,8,16,32,64} membership test, ScpiError(-224) is raised before assignment, and clock_divider keeps its prior value. The probe checks == 1 because on a fresh device the divider is still the reset default.'}, {t:'The divider is clamped to the nearest reachable value, 64',c:false,w:'No coercion happens anywhere in this model — validation is strict membership, and rejected writes leave state untouched.'}, {t:'128 is stored — it is a power of two like the rest of the set',c:false,w:'That was the pre-fix defect. Being a power of two is irrelevant; what matters is that no ID×TAIDEX product reaches 128.'}, {t:'-222 is queued because 128 exceeds the range maximum of 64',c:false,w:'The handler raises -224, not -222: the divider is an enumerated value set (membership check), not a continuous numeric range. Note the audit prose loosely says "rejected"; the code is the authority.'}, ] }, {id:'e3',ch:'enc',type:'mc', q:'Hardware CAN divide by 48 (ID=8 × TAIDEX=6), yet TIMERA0:CLOCK:DIVIDER 48 is rejected. Is that a compliance bug?', opts:[ {t:'No — the model exposes the power-of-two subset {1,2,4,8,16,32,64} of the reachable products; refusing a reachable value is a documented simplification, unlike accepting an unreachable one',c:true, w:'Correct. The two error directions are asymmetric. Accepting /128 (unreachable) lets SIL tests validate impossible hardware — a compliance bug. Rejecting /48 (reachable but unexposed) merely narrows the model; a test hits a loud -224 and the limitation is discoverable. Every accepted value is achievable in silicon, which is the invariant that matters.'}, {t:'Yes — the model must accept every value the hardware can produce',c:false,w:'Completeness is desirable but its absence fails loudly (-224 at the call site). The audit reserves ACCEPTS_INVALID/NON_COMPLIANT for the silent direction: accepting what hardware cannot do.'}, {t:'Yes — 48 is rejected with the wrong error code',c:false,w:'-224 is the right code for a value outside the accepted set; the question is whether the set should include 48, and that is a scope choice, not a code-selection issue.'}, {t:'No — /48 is not actually reachable, because TAIDEX only takes powers of two',c:false,w:'TAIDEX is a 3-bit field covering 1 through 8 including 6 — /48 = 8×6 is genuinely reachable. The model still doesn\'t expose it, by design.'}, ] }, {id:'e4',ch:'enc',type:'mc', q:'Which pair correctly matches each rejected write to its SCPI error code?', opts:[ {t:'COUNT 0x10000 → -222 (out of range); CC1:MODE BANANA → -224 (illegal value)',c:true, w:'Correct. -222 "Data out of range" is for numeric magnitudes outside the representable range (width guards on COUNT/CCR). -224 "Illegal parameter value" is for set-membership failures (CC mode tokens, the divider set, timer MODE).'}, {t:'COUNT 0x10000 → -224; CC1:MODE BANANA → -222',c:false,w:'Reversed. Range violations take -222; membership violations take -224.'}, {t:'Both are -222 — every bad parameter is out of range',c:false,w:'BANANA is not "out of range" — it is not in the CC mode value set {COMPARE, CAPTURE} at all. That classification difference is exactly what the two codes encode.'}, {t:'Both are -224 — every bad parameter is an illegal value',c:false,w:'The width guards deliberately use -222: the parameter type and set are fine, the magnitude is not representable in 16 bits.'}, ] }, {id:'e5',ch:'enc',type:'w', q:'State the general reachability principle for device simulators: how do register field widths bound the reachable state space, and why does accepting an unreachable state void SIL results? Use ID×TAIDEX and the old /128 acceptance as your example.', c:[{l:'an n-bit field encodes at most 2^n values; derived settings are bounded by the encodings',t:['2^n','2**n','finite','bounded','at most','encodings']}, {l:'reachable state space = values some encoding actually produces',t:['reachable','produce','combination','product']}, {l:'accepted set must be a subset of the reachable set',t:['subset','mirror','no more','only reachable','must not accept']}, {l:'unreachable state → downstream results describe hardware that cannot exist → silently void',t:['void','silently','cannot exist','impossible','fiction','meaningless','invalid']}], m:`An n-bit register field encodes at most 2^n values, so any setting derived from fields is bounded by what the encodings can jointly produce. The reachable state space is the set of values SOME combination actually reaches — for the timer divider, the 20 products of ID {1,2,4,8} × TAIDEX {1..8}, max /64. A simulator's accepted set must be a subset of that reachable set. The moment it accepts a value outside it — the old VALID set's 128 — the simulated device enters a configuration no silicon can occupy. Nothing crashes: the danger is precisely that the simulation keeps answering queries, ticking through test steps, and passing assertions. Every result computed downstream of the impossible state (tick frequencies, period counts, timing margins) describes imaginary hardware, so the SIL run is void without ever saying so. The firmware bug it should have caught — asking for /128 — instead surfaces on the bench, where the real part's fields silently hold something else. Reject early (-222/-224) and the failure is loud, local, and diagnosable in simulation.` }, // BANK-APPEND
